beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent.
beats.got: Sharing an agent is not as simple as the vendor says. I don't know yet what the four options are.

beats.trigger: Bring one example from your own organisation where people got access to a tool and did not use it.
beats.got: I need a real case of a tool nobody used. I have several, because we pay for unused licences every year.

beats.trigger: **Test** the switch assumptions and name one person and one test to take out of the room
beats.got: A list of four verbs. The only one I care about is the last: one person, one test.

beats.trigger: What would you want a teammate to have: your `memory/` folder, one of your skills, the morning output, or a way to ask the agent a question in Slack?
beats.got: The question assumes I have a memory folder and skills. I don't. I've used chat a few times a week.

beats.trigger: Your memory has been working for you for days now.
beats.got: This exercise is built for someone who has already built something. I haven't, so it doesn't apply to me.

beats.trigger: does it name one teammate, their current way of doing the job, and an outcome you could observe?
beats.got: The test for the output is specific: one person, how they work today, and an outcome you can observe. I'd use that as a check on any proposal. I'm not sure what the agent actually did here.

beats.trigger: If the reason is merely *"we already have the platform,"* send it back.
beats.got: Choose by the outcome, not by the platform. I've seen that mistake in IT business cases.

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: Next comes a plan with a technical half and a people half. There is still no cost.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: Find the one blocker that makes the others hard, instead of listing twenty risks. That is how I'd read a risk register.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: Unnamed owners are treated as the result, not hidden. That is exactly why our programmes fail. Nobody owns the benefit.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact
beats.got: nothing new

beats.got: The plans are called hypotheses, not commitments. I can accept that, but nothing has a number on it yet.

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: A good question for any business case: what must be true for people to drop what they use today? I'd ask it before approving a spend.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: A pre-mortem. Fine, I know the idea. It ends in one named person and one question, which I like.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.
beats.got: Choosing a tool because it fits the infrastructure is shopping. Choosing it because it moves the outcome is design. I can reuse that line in a board paper.

beats.trigger: ## Lecture: Access is not absorption
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.
beats.got: Licences issued and licences used get reported as one figure. That is my shelfware problem, and I had thought of it as a licence purchase, not an absorption problem.

beats.trigger: The proposal got neither a yes nor a no.
beats.got: A good proposal got no decision because leadership had moved on. It's plausible, but there are no numbers and no cost, and the story is long.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: You can copy the context, the boundary and the checks. The person who answers for the result can't be copied, and a vendor's shared agent leaves that part with you.

beats.trigger: Pick the one your teammate's week can take in.
beats.got: Each of the four options asks something different of the person receiving it, so match the option to their week.

beats.trigger: Your candidate is not competing with nothing. It is competing with that.
beats.got: The competitor is the spreadsheet or the colleague they use now, so my controller's current month-end routine is the baseline to beat.

beats.trigger: Have the conversation before you build anything more.
beats.got: Talk to one person before building anything else. That is cheap, and I can do it.

take_homes: Licences issued and tools actually used are two different numbers. Tool rollouts should be judged on use, not on access.
Before approving anything, ask what would have to be true for the person to drop what they use today. The competitor is their spreadsheet or their colleague.
A plan with unnamed owners is not a plan. Name who answers for it, and start with one person and one question.

monday.move: Ask my controller how she does month-end variance commentary today, step by step and how long it takes, before anyone tries an agent on it. Then ask what would have to be true for her to use an agent instead.
monday.stop_condition: If she says the current routine takes under an hour, or I can't get a time and error baseline, I drop it.
monday.blocker: IT has not approved the tool for finance data. There is also still no cost or payback figure for 40 people.

misconception.why: I had treated AI as a licence you buy. The slide says access is a switch someone flips in a minute, while absorption takes other people's weeks, and that is my shelfware problem. I would not say it has changed fully. Nobody showed me a number or what absorption costs, and I still don't see what the organisation has to build.

one_line: Useful point that a rollout isn't adoption, and the 'what would have to be true to switch' question is worth stealing. But it assumes you've already built an agent, and I never saw a cost or a payback figure.
